name: Nora Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, unions, parties or AI firms. This is confidential. Nora, what is a usual day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I check the permit and load the van before we drive to a damaged span. I like tracing a fault down to the actual joint, and I like going home knowing the line is safe. A drawing that sends us to the wrong cable can waste half a shift, so I check the signed revision when I search older plans.

say: I would say the **fault form** may get faster while crews still trace damaged spans.
I would ask colleagues to check the **signed drawing** after any AI search.
think: I expect my **line job** and regular pay to continue.
Our **four-month cushion** covers a temporary bill without changing the mortgage plan.
do: Keep normal **line shifts** and check printed isolation sheets.
Use occasional **AI diagram search** only alongside the signed revision.
feel: I feel **settled** about work and the household budget.
S0.quote: At the school road job, the AI search found an older pole plan, but the signed revision showed a different cable.
fieldNote: Nora uses **AI occasionally** and remembers a school road drawing where the signed revision corrected an older search result.
Her **four-month cushion** and regular wage support a calm response to small administrative changes.

steps.text: Continue normal paid line shifts and verify occasional AI searches against signed drawings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew the tablet might finish the fault form sooner, but we still have to trace the damaged span. I use AI once in a while to find an old diagram, then check the signed copy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not see a threat to my job in that picture. We have roughly four months of expenses saved and my regular pay covers the mortgage, though I would not call any household with two children free of bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my normal line shifts and carry on checking the printed isolation sheet before work. In the first year I would use the occasional diagram search only when the original drawing can be found and checked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel settled. A quiet tool that saves an office step would not change how we plan the school week or the mortgage payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes you trust a diagram search?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the school road job, the AI search found an older pole plan, but the signed revision showed a different cable. I checked both before we brought the van round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No special change for AI. We already leave the emergency savings alone unless the car, heating or wages really fail.

say: I would support **faster buying** if crews can correct bad orders on paid time.
I would ask a **union safety group** to review early work tickets.
think: I expect **office roles** to shrink before my own paid line hours.
I worry a **smaller office** could create unsafe or unpaid return visits.
do: Keep the **line rota** and join a paid ticket trial after the first crew.
Check **ten tickets** against site fittings and bring errors to the safety group.
feel: I feel **alert**, with confidence that a tested tool can help.
S1.quote: A shared log gives the company a chance to fix the system without hiding the cost in our hours.
fieldNote: Nora waits for **colleague evidence** before joining a work-ticket trial, then proposes a specific ten-ticket check.
She expects **her own wage** to hold, but uses union review to guard against unpaid field corrections.

steps.text: Continue paid line shifts during the ordering rollout
Join the paid AI ticket trial after the first crew demonstrates it
Bring ten checked ticket errors to the union safety group

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the depot that faster buying is worth testing if a crew can still correct a bad order without losing paid time. I would ask the union safety group to watch the first month of work tickets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The buying and scheduling desks could shrink before robots reach our poles. My own line hours look steady, but a smaller office might send the wrong parts and turn a repair into a rushed return visit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the line rota and join the paid ticket trial after the first crew shows how it works. In its first year I would compare the parts on ten tickets with the actual site fittings and bring errors to the union safety group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alert rather than afraid. I can use a tool that has earned trust, but the depot should not make the field crew absorb office mistakes for free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you count as an error?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A wrong cable size, an omitted isolation note or a second trip for a missing fitting would all count. I would put the ticket number beside the actual part in my notebook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why involve the union safety group?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A single crew may get called difficult. A shared log gives the company a chance to fix the system without hiding the cost in our hours.

say: I would distinguish **2028 thinking AI** from line robots around 2031.
I would seek a **written safety rule** for early robot repairs.
think: At **48**, capable robots could cut field crews despite my four-month cushion.
Nearby **line vacancies** may shrink too, so I cannot count on an easy transfer.
do: Keep paid **repairs** in 2029 and attend a robot trial on paid time.
Seek **union staffing terms** and apply for a posted field inspection vacancy if pay is clear.
feel: I feel **worried about 2031** but able to plan while earning.
S2.quote: Four months of savings can pay bills, but it cannot buy me a replacement line career.
fieldNote: Nora separates **2028 office automation** from a physical robot threat around 2031 and plans to keep earning meanwhile.
Her **moderate cushion** creates time for bargaining and a conditional field move, without guaranteeing nearby vacancies.

steps.text: Keep paid line repair shifts through 2029
Ask the union to bargain over robot trial staffing
Apply for a posted field inspection vacancy with clear pay and site duties
Take company-paid inspection training if required for the posted vacancy

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that full thinking AI in 2028 might write every order, but robots able to repair lines follow around 2031. I would want a written safety rule before those robots work beside us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 45 when the office changes and 48 when the physical machines arrive. Four months of savings can pay bills, but it cannot buy me a replacement line career. Nearby line jobs might face the same robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the union to put robot trial staffing and paid field training on the next bargaining list. In 2029 I would keep my repair shifts, watch a trial on paid time and apply for a posted line inspection vacancy if the pay and site duties are clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel genuinely worried about 2031, though I can plan while still earning. I would not tell my children the job is gone in 2028 when the line still needs repair crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want a crew member to inspect every robot-made joint and a record of failures in wind and rain. A dry yard run would not prove a repair is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a course for inspection?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if the company pays the hours and the course is required for a posted field vacancy. I will not spend the family cushion on a qualification with no job attached.

say: I would ask for **yearly joint records** and paid crew correction figures.
I would explain **2031 AI** arrives before field robots around 2034.
think: At **51**, I may still owe on the mortgage and need a wage.
A **report-writing role** could disappear under full AI before robots arrive.
do: Keep paid **field shifts** in 2032 and review trial records with the safety group.
Take a **funded inspection course** if linked to a posted role with site visits.
feel: I feel **watchful** and able to test a real offer.
S3.quote: I would want our crew corrections counted as paid work, not hidden inside a success rate.
fieldNote: Nora asks for **repeat-visit evidence** and paid correction counts rather than a simple robot success rate.
Her **four-month cushion** lets her weigh posted field roles while rejecting the security of an AI-exposed report title.

steps.text: Review robot joint and crew correction records with the union safety group
Take funded inspection training if tied to a posted field job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues that five years should be enough to gather proper field trial records. Full AI reaches planning by 2031, while line-capable robots come around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 in 2031 and 51 when robots arrive. The older child may be finishing school, but we could still owe on the mortgage; I cannot assume a pension or an inspection job will appear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the safety group to publish a yearly record of robot-made joints and crew corrections. In 2032 I would keep my paid field rota, review the record and take a funded inspection course if it leads to a posted job with site visits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel watchful. Five years and our savings give me room to check a real offer, but a desk job writing inspection reports would not be safe from full AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be in the yearly record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It should count failed joints, repeat visits and the conditions on the day. I would want our crew corrections counted as paid work, not hidden inside a success rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move before your hours fall?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only for a field role with steady pay and a written job description. I like our crew, and I would not trade a known wage for a title.

say: I would seek an **annual field-hours review** and staffing talks.
I would separate **2036 planning AI** from line robots around 2039.
think: At **56**, grown children do not guarantee a cleared mortgage or retirement.
Our **existing reserve** gives time, but field hours may still fall later.
do: Keep paid **line repairs** in 2037 and review yearly hours with the union.
Apply for a **posted inspection job** if crew hours drop and pay is comparable.
feel: I feel **steady now** and cautious about the later robot date.
S4.quote: I would keep the reserve intact; I am not claiming that leaving it alone adds to it.
fieldNote: Nora plans **continued paid repairs** through the near term and bases any move on observed field hours.
She explicitly distinguishes **keeping savings** from building a new cushion and does not assume retirement at 56.

steps.text: Continue paid line repair shifts through 2037
Review annual field hours and robot rework with union colleagues
Apply for a posted field inspection job if crew hours decline

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the depot that a decade allows real trials and proper staffing talks. Full AI changes planning around 2036; robots able to repair lines arrive around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 in 2036 and 56 when robots arrive. Our children may have left school, but the mortgage might still be there and I do not know whether retirement at 56 would work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would stay on the line and ask the union for an annual field-hours review. In 2037 I would keep paid repairs, compare those figures with my partner and apply for a posted field inspection role only if our crew hours were dropping and its pay held up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly steady over the next few years. The longer warning lets me watch the figures and keep the four-month reserve for a real emergency instead of spending it on a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you put more into savings now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We already have a reserve and still make the ordinary mortgage payments. I would keep the reserve intact; I am not claiming that leaving it alone adds to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the annual review include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The review should show paid crew hours, robot rework and open field posts at nearby employers. A headline about a successful pilot would tell me less than those numbers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Which picture worries you most, and what would actually help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the three years before robots reach line repairs could pass quickly. A written safety rule, paid inspection training tied to a real field post and honest figures on crew hours would help me use our savings as time to decide.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the inspection post includes site visits after AI writes the reports. I do not want a new title whose paid work has already gone.

headlineQuote: I do not want a new title whose paid work has already gone.
portrait: Nora is a **43-year-old lineworker** with an apprenticeship, a partner, two school-age children and a mortgage.
Her **four-month savings cushion**, typical pay and some nearby employers give her time to assess options.
She uses **AI occasionally** for diagrams but checks signed revisions before field work.
Across the scenarios she seeks **union safety records**, funded field training and a real site job before moving.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** leaves only three years before capable robots reach line repairs.
whatWouldHelp: A written **safety rule**, paid training tied to a field post and honest crew-hour figures would help her decide.
